literal_evidence.quote:
In the experiment described below we replicate the Bock
and Lobell (1990) ditrjinsitive experiment, but include a
third prime condition, the 'fulfilling' frame (Levin, 1993),
exemplified in example (3):

Our hypothesis is that the semantic similarity
between the 'provide-with' form and the ditransitive will
lead to an increase in ditransitive responses after a 'provide-with' prime. Since the two differ in their syntactic
form, the predicted effect would not be attributable to
strictly syntactic processes, and would argue that semantic
factors as well as form-based factors influence the priming
effect.

These results can be interpreted as showing that conceptual dissimilarity has no effect on structural priming.
Note, however, that the semantics of the two constructions are not all that dissimilar. Although in (1) the object of to is a locative, while in (2) it is a benefactive,
there is considerable linguistic evidence showing that both
these roles are subsumed under the larger category of goal
(Jackendoff 1972; Lakoff and Johnson 1980; Goldberg
1995).There are cases such as The widow sent a package
to the church , where the argument church falls some208 where intermediate between a pure locative and a pure
benefactive. In addition there is a substantial evidence for
a general metaphor, TRANSFE R O F POSSESSION as
PHYSICAL TRANSFER , that involves transfer of possession without physical transfer, and involves the prepositions to, from and away. (e.g. She received the house
from her mother's estate. I He gave the house away.)
Thus it is not entirely clear from these data whether the
priming is due only to form-based factors, or to a combination of form and meaning.
literal_evidence.note: Retains raw control characters, page-number insertion, line breaks and spelling; no repair.

literal_evidence.quote:
Intransitive sentences were used as an additional
condition in order to assess preferences for the two alternative forms after a minimally related sentence type.

There were 32 %
more ditransitive responses after ditransitive primes than
after dative primes (and conversely 32 % more dative responses after dative primes than after ditransitive primes).
In addition, were 28 % more ditransitive responses after
provide-with primes than after datives.

Planned comparisons were run to test the experimental
hypothesis. T-tests showed significantly fewer ditransitive responses and more dative responses after dative prime
than after either ditransitive (p < .01 for both subjects &
items) or provide-with primes (p < .05) but no difference
in the percentage of ditransitive responses after ditransitive
and provide-with primes (p > .1).

Finally, we tested whether there was a significant difference between ditransitive and prepostional object responses following an intransitive prime. In the items
analysis the ditransitive mean was 56% , while the prepositional object was 44% . This difference is not significant (p > 1) confirming that Bock's finding of no independent preference for either clause type was also true of
our items. Although in the subjects analysis the difference
was larger, again it did not reach significance (p =.092).
W e will return to this point in the general discussion.
literal_evidence.note: Contains literal p > 1 and raw control characters; retained as written, without numerical repair.

literal_evidence.quote:
The present experiment indicates that the mapping of semantic features to syntactic positions in a prime sentence
has an effect on the production of a target sentence. This
finding is especially striking in light of the fact that a
purely syntactic account of such priming would have expected target sentences to be produced with a matching
syntactic form.

Other explanations for these effects are possible, of
course. In earlier work looking at the active/passive alternation. Bock has shown indejjendent effects of both
animacy (a semantic factor) and structure on syntactic
priming. Given the facts of the ditransitive alternation it
is hard to tease apart the effects of animacy order from
those of the mapping of conceptual features like thematic
roles to syntactic positions - other than in exceptional
cases, the object one of a ditransitive must be animate, as
is the direct object of the provide-with construction.
Given this, it is reasonable to ask if animacy order is what
leads to the effects w e find here.
In the current experiment there are three prime conditions:
One in which both animacy and structure are consistent
with the ditransitive, one in which bodi are consistent
with the prepositional dative, and a third which pits the
two against each other: animacy is consistent with the
ditransitive while structure is consistent with prepositional dative. If indeed these should show independent,
additive effects, then the third condition should be influenced by both, resulting in behavior somewhere between
the other two prime conditions. However, this is not the
case. Instead, the third condition patterns closely with the
ditransitive, and is significantly different from the prepositional dative.
Given these results, one would have to conclude either
that the earlier animacy account is incorrect, or, more
plausibly, that what is operative here is a different factor,
the order of expression of coarse semantic roles.
literal_evidence.note: Explicit alternative explanation and authors’ reasoning; attribution of earlier animacy findings must not be silently collapsed into the 1990 dative experiment.

literal_evidence.quote:
It should be noted that in the present experiment the responses in the prepositional dative condition are significantly different from those in the ditransitive, but the datives do not 'prime' dative picture descriptions in the
sense that a strong majority of responses after this prime
are dative. In fact, only 55 % of the responses are. While
this does not affect the results, it is an interesting point
and worth investigation. On e explanation consistent with
210 the current data is that the ditransitive may serve as the
default construction for many speakers, from which they
are primed away in the prepositional dative condition. If
this were true, a purely structural account would predict
that subjects should equally be primed by the structure of
provide-with condition. However, this was not the case.
Even on this account, then, semantics must still be involved: The structural prime only has an effect only
when it combines both the syntax and the semantics of
the prepositional dative.
literal_evidence.note: Preserves an internal inconsistency: Table 2 labels 55 as percent ditransitive after dative prime; this paragraph says 55 percent are dative. Neither reading repaired.

literal_evidence.quote:
The coarse mapping of conceptual features to syntactic
positions demonstrated to affect priming in this experiment can account for much of the existing data on "syntactic" priming, including the ability of locative 'to' constructions to prime dative 'to' discussed above: in both
cases the theme appears as object and the goal appears in a
prepositional phrase marked by to. The finding that benefactives {Pat baked a cake for Chris) prime datives {Pat
served a cake to Chris) (Bock 1986), can be accounted for
similarly, since in both cases the theme argument appears
as direct object. The distinction between benefactives and
goals/recipients is apparently not strong enough to prevent the priming.
literal_evidence.note: Claims a semantic-role account can explain the existing locative-to-dative result, not that that empirical result disappeared.

literal_evidence.quote:
More work is required to fully account for the priming
of passives by intransitive locatives such as The priest
was standing by the stained glass window (Bock & Loebell 1990). As this example illustrates, the Bock and
Loebell study used locative sentences that contained the
same be auxiliary and preposition by that appear in passives. Experiments are being designed to determine
whether expressions that have the same syntactic form but
different morphemes, such as The priest might stand near
the stained glass window, actually prime passives as predicted by a purely syntactic account. It may be that some
conceptual or morphological overlap is required for structural priming. (See also Dell et al. (in press) for a model
of this locative data that in the spirit of the present analysis.).
literal_evidence.note: Future experiments described here are not completed tests in this paper.

literal_evidence.section: Discussion (closing paragraph; no separate Conclusion heading)
literal_evidence.quote:
Thus it seems that "syntactic priming" may be fundamentally influenced by elements of conceptual features or semantic roles. This suggests that rather than being purely
syntactic, the phenomenon might be at the level of the
mapping between semantics and syntax.

original_visual_evidence.reading: Page 1 prints Framing sentences, Kathryn Bock and Helga Loebell, Cognition 35 (1990) 1-39; received August 2, 1988 and final revision accepted May 11, 1989. Page 39 ends the references. The file contains 39 pages and the PDF metadata title is PII: 0010-0277(90)90035-I. PubMed gives both authors, title, journal, year, pages and requested DOI. original_visual_evidence.reading: The original explicitly contrasts form mapping and meaning mapping. Under message-linked construction, thematically matching primes should prime more strongly; under syntactic categorization divorced from conceptual relations, frames that match syntactically should prime comparably despite event-role changes. Experiments 1 and 2 are presented as tests of these predictions, with Experiment 3 testing a metrical/closed-class alternative. Thus semantic independence is an experimentally investigated published interpretation, not only a later generic theory attributed to the article.
original_visual_evidence.limit: Paraphrase of visible scanned pages, not a literal quotation and not eligible as an offset-backed quotation.

original_visual_evidence.reading: Experiment 1: 96 undergraduates; 30 sentence triplets and 30 dative-event pictures. Three primes: prepositional dative, prepositional locative, double-object dative control. Dative and locative share theme as direct object and a to-phrase, with beneficiary versus location as prepositional object. Double-object controls reverse object ordering; verb differs to avoid privileging lexical overlap. Results: 202 prepositional/429 double-object responses after dative, 223/417 after locative, 159/485 after double-object control. Dative and locative each differ reliably from control, but not from each other. Discussion interprets comparable repetition despite event-role change; the numerical locative advantage is nonsignificant. There is no provide-with condition in this original condition set.
original_visual_evidence.limit: Paraphrase of visible scanned pages, not a literal quotation and not eligible as an offset-backed quotation.

original_visual_evidence.reading: The 1990 discussion raises whether double-object primes merely reduce prepositional responses rather than both alternatives priming. It appeals to Experiment 1 in Bock (1986), which included an intransitive condition with prepositional-dative production midway between the two prime types. This is a prior-study comparison within the 1990 report, not a 1990 intransitive condition, and it does not establish a 50/50 no-preference null. The current paper attributes its null to Bock without a year in that result sentence. Original Bock 1986 was not recovered in this task, so that attribution remains unverified against its own primary text.
original_visual_evidence.limit: Paraphrase of visible scanned pages, not a literal quotation and not eligible as an offset-backed quotation.

original_visual_evidence.reading: The original itself notes that beneficiaries and moved-to locations can both be classified as goal arguments, allowing their conceptual similarity to explain Experiment 1. Experiment 2 is explicitly introduced to address that concern using a stronger contrast between agency and location. It also notes a possible preceding-trial contamination of the nonsignificant locative advantage and lengthens the intertrial interval from 8 to 12 items. This anticipates an important part of the later dative/locative construct critique.
original_visual_evidence.limit: Paraphrase of visible scanned pages, not a literal quotation and not eligible as an offset-backed quotation.

original_visual_evidence.reading: Experiment 2: 96 campus participants; 18 sentence triplets: full passive with by-agent, locative with by-location and progressive verb, active control. Passive and locative share auxiliary and preposition, but differ in event-role assignments. Transitive pictures contain a nonhuman usually inanimate agent and human patient. Passive responses: 285/360 after passive, 281/351 after locative, 252/350 after active control; passive and locative each yield significantly more passives than active control, and do not differ significantly from each other. Active-response comparisons are less uniform and include nonsignificant subject contrasts. Authors treat the passive-response results as a conceptual-role contrast supporting structural priming; the current study does not collect new passive/locative data.
original_visual_evidence.limit: Paraphrase of visible scanned pages, not a literal quotation and not eligible as an offset-backed quotation.

original_visual_evidence.reading: Experiment 3 uses the same subjects/lists as Experiment 2. Primes are prepositional dative, infinitive, double-object control. Dative and infinitive match through to and in syllable/stress patterns but differ in constituent structure. Prepositional responses: 140/301 after dative, 108/315 after infinitive, 109/337 after double-object control. Dative exceeds the other prime types significantly for subjects/items. Double-object versus infinitive difference is not significant; the authors acknowledge this qualification. It tests a rhythm/closed-class alternative to syntax, not provide-with semantics.

original_visual_evidence.reading: General discussion restricts the claim to some procedures and certain conceptual features; the tested event-role changes had no readily detectable impact. Page 35 expressly allows thematic relations to matter earlier, before constituent representations are formed, and discusses semantically differentiated elements being linked to syntactic roles in a distinguishable operation. Conclusion distinguishes the roles of things in events (the tested meanings) from other meanings implicated in language and thought, and limits the claim to the explored domain of phrase-encoding oblique objects. Different sorts of meaning may affect different sorts of structure. Do not equate the original with a universal claim that semantics never affects production.

conditional_scope_distinctions.question: Was semantic independence an experimentally tested original claim?
conditional_scope_distinctions.source_based_distinction: The original tests variation in event roles while retaining constituent structure, and interprets the null difference as evidence for separable syntactic construction. This claim is published and experimentally motivated, but qualified to tested contrasts/processes; it is stronger than merely observing a dative effect and weaker than universally excluding semantics.

conditional_scope_distinctions.question: Which original empirical finding is tested again in the current data?
conditional_scope_distinctions.source_based_distinction: The current dative versus ditransitive comparison corresponds to the original Experiment 1 contrast, with the same directional difference. Current planned comparisons explicitly report the difference. The current data do not repeat the original locative-to-dative contrast, passive/locative contrast, or metrical/infinitive contrast. The new provide-with prime separates coarse semantic-role order from constituent form using a condition absent from the original.

conditional_scope_distinctions.question: Is provide-with only an extension, or a test bearing on an original interpretation?
conditional_scope_distinctions.source_based_distinction: At the condition level it is an added extension. At the claim level the authors explicitly design it against constituent-structure-only priming and use the finding to argue for semantic involvement. If scope is the repeated dative/ditransitive empirical contrast, this additional result is not a disagreement on that contrast. If scope includes semantic independence inferred from original conceptual contrasts, it is a new operational test bearing on that interpretation, rather than a direct rerun of the original semantic-independence manipulation. Whether these are commensurate claims remains a scientific scope question; no outcome code assigned.

conditional_scope_distinctions.question: Do the current authors make a construct-validity argument while retaining original effects?
conditional_scope_distinctions.source_based_distinction: Their introduction questions whether locative versus benefactive distinguishes meaning, because both can be goals; their discussion explains the existing locative-to-dative effect through coarse semantic-role mapping. This is a substantive interpretation/construct argument, not a report that the original locative effect failed to appear in new data. The main discussion emphasizes semantic-to-syntactic mapping rather than a technical failure of this experiment. The original already acknowledges the goal objection and uses Experiment 2 to address it; the current authors leave that passive/locative effect for future work and possible morphological/conceptual overlap. No explicit current overall verdict on the replication as a whole was located. Whether this central interpretive critique constitutes a codebook special verdict is reserved for parent/expert judgment.

conditional_scope_distinctions.question: What does the intransitive result establish about this original?
conditional_scope_distinctions.source_based_distinction: Current authors explicitly say the nonsignificant item difference confirms Bock’s lack of independent clause preference. However, the recovered 1990 report appeals to Bock 1986 for an intransitive condition and describes an intermediate baseline, not equal alternatives. Treat the current statement as an explicit author comparison with uncertain original-paper scope, not as a verified 1990 null result.

remaining_ambiguities_and_limits: Recovered PDF is a complete-looking published scan, not an author manuscript or publisher HTML. Identity is triangulated by visible title/authors/year/page span, PDF PII metadata, and PubMed DOI. Formal byte identity with the publisher distribution was not established.

Embedded PDF OCR is severely incomplete (16463 Unicode characters across 39 page delimiters). Original page readings are explicitly paraphrases tied to image hashes, not silently repaired quote evidence. Exact original literal excerpts are supplied from the independently fetched PubMed abstract. It is not possible to provide complete raw UTF-8 original-body clauses for the page-17 and page-35/36 qualifications from this extraction without introducing new transcription/OCR; none was done.

The original abstract is an indexed author abstract, not full body text; it alone cannot establish condition details or author qualifications. Those are documented via visual readings of the new full primary PDF.

Current text has literal control U+0002 within words, OCR spellings, a p > 1 report, and conflicting 55-percent wording between table and discussion. They are retained exactly, and no sign, digit or character repair is used.
The current Results passage calls the dependent variables ditransitives and double-object responses; this terminology is preserved, not silently corrected to prepositional versus double-object.

Current same-condition significance and the added provide-with comparison do not by themselves establish an author-stated overall replication verdict. The theoretical scope of the original experimental claim versus its later strongest interpretation must remain separate.

Current discussion considers animacy as an alternative and rejects a simple independent additive account because provide-with clusters with ditransitive. This does not experimentally isolate every possible semantic/morphological account.
Original Bock 1986 full report was not acquired; the exact original baseline-null claim remains unverified. The 1990 source explicitly locates its intransitive support in 1986.
Original passive/locative and infinitive controls are not rerun by Hare/Goldberg. New experiments proposed in their discussion cannot be treated as completed contradictions.

Original theoretical qualifications permit some semantic effects before constituent building and outside the explored phrase-encoding domain. Whether the current semantic-order result contradicts that qualified mechanistic claim or changes its operational scope is not settled by a title or a single returning effect.
